paras: The lynching of John Wagoner took place at Ironton, Lawrence County, Ohio, shortly after midnight on the night of January 19, 1882, when forty to sixty masked men took him from the county jail and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard. Wagoner was charged with murdering Dr. Joseph A. Beggs; his co-accused, William Zeek, was strung up by the same band and returned to jail after a forced confession. No one was arrested, and Ohio papers divided over whether the hanging was justified.

Beggs, described as bookkeeper and chemist at the Alice furnace, was killed with a shotgun near Ironton on a Wednesday night at the end of November 1881. John Wagner and Bill Seek were arrested, and according to a December 2 report Wagner admitted firing two shots at Beggs but said he had acted in self-defense. At the coroner's inquest the accused said a man calling himself "Old Hell" was shot at Wagoner's house when he would not leave.
The Cincinnati Commercial's correspondent wrote that there had been threats of lynching from the start and that the community was "almost desperate" over murderers who had escaped through juries.

A few minutes after midnight the sheriff answered a knock at the jail and was seized at revolver point; when he refused to give up the keys, his wife surrendered them. Wagoner and Zeek were led from their shared cell; according to the Eaton Democrat, Wagoner protested "I didn't mean to kill him" and was hanged to a tree a few feet from the court-house within two minutes.

Zeek was swung up with a rope around his neck, confessed, and was returned to his cell. In the Ironton dispatch he spoke of an organized band for murder and robbery and named Sarah Zeek, Wagoner or Frank Marshall as the killer, while the Eaton Democrat and the Jackson Standard reported that he named Wagoner, his brother-in-law.

The masked lynchers answered to numbers and took orders from a leader and squad captains. Guards held passersby until the hanging was done, and the band then dispersed, in one account leaving in wagons. The body hung until morning, when the coroner viewed it and had it cut down.

Mrs. Zeek and a Mrs. Hall were arrested the next morning on the strength of Zeek's confession. By January 31 no one had been arrested for the lynching, and Mrs. Zeek and Marshall had been discharged because Zeek refused to make a sworn statement against them. In March the Jackson Standard reported that the grand jury had declined to indict Zeek, finding no sufficient evidence outside his confession.
At nearby Catlettsburg, Kentucky, guards kept a stricter watch over the Ashland murder defendants after the lynching.

Dispatches from Ironton and Cincinnati ran on January 21 in papers from St. Paul and Cheyenne to Dallas and Los Angeles, calling Wagoner "the murderer" or "one of the murderers" of Dr. Biggs. The Times-Star version closed by saying that "public opinion apparently approves the act," a line repeated in the Perrysburg Journal along with the remark that "The prisoners bore bad characters."

The Cincinnati Commercial's correspondent wrote that "the slow process of the law was dispensed with" by "intelligent men," not a mob "of the rabble," and the paper's editorial called the hanging a "prelude" if the law were not enforced more sternly. Reprinting those passages, the Memphis Public Ledger mocked lynching "in the glorious climate of Ohio" and judged that Wagoner "deserved hanging, but the mob had no more right."

Ohio editors split: the Jackson Standard declared that "this was right" and preferred "Judge Lynch" to the modern jury. The Stark County Democrat called the lynching "all wrong," noting it was the second in Ohio after one in Athens County, and the Spirit of Democracy at Woodsfield condemned papers that encouraged mob law. None of the reports mentioned the race of Wagoner or Zeek.

The Ironton dispatches put the lynching on the night of January 19, after midnight, while later summaries said Friday night or the 20th. The Times-Star version said the band let Zeek "live for the present," which one summary rendered as letting him go, but the Ironton dispatch and later reports said he was returned to jail.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A band of masked men took John Wagoner, a prisoner accused of murder, from the Ironton jail and hanged him in the court-house yard (A5, A8, A18).

Forty to sixty masked men took Wagoner from the sheriff's custody by force and hanged him (A8, A18), and the Commercial's correspondent and the Jackson Standard framed the act as justice for the murder of Dr. Beggs that the courts had failed to deliver (A11, A16). The papers do not state Wagoner's race.

Independent Ironton dispatches to the Cincinnati Times-Star, the Cincinnati Commercial and a separate Ironton wire agree on the taking from jail and the hanging in the court-house yard (A5, A8, A11, A18).

accounts.label: Times-Star Ironton special
accounts.gist: Forty to sixty masked men took Wagoner out between 12 and 1, made Zeek confess, let him live, and left in wagons; public opinion apparently approved.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial special
accounts.gist: A drilled band of not more than forty or fifty masked, numbered men acted with 'the regularity of macinery' after years of murderers escaping juries.

accounts.label: Eaton Democrat narrative
accounts.gist: The sheriff was overpowered, his wife gave up the keys, Wagoner protested he did not mean to kill and was hanged within two minutes; Zeek said Wagoner did the killing.

accounts.label: Defendants at the inquest
accounts.gist: The accused said a man calling himself 'Old Hell' came to Wagoner's house and was shot when he would not leave; Wagner claimed self-defense.

framing.detail: Cincinnati and Ironton dispatches called Wagoner 'the murderer' or 'one of the murderers' of Dr. Biggs and reported that public opinion approved.
The Commercial's Ironton correspondent wrote of 'speedy, inflexible justice' by 'intelligent men' and called it no mob 'of the rabble'.
The Memphis Public Ledger mocked Ohio ('in the glorious climate of Ohio') and said Wagoner 'no doubt, deserved hanging, but the mob had no more right'.
The Jackson Standard's 'More Lynch Law' said 'this was right' and preferred Judge Lynch to juries.
The Stark County Democrat called the lynching 'all wrong' and the second Ohio case after Athens County.
The Spirit of Democracy condemned papers that encouraged mob law and noted the Athens County lynchers went unpunished.
Brief news columns in California, Kentucky and Missouri ran one-line items on the lynching.
